content: Dimenhydrinate, fluconazole (oral and injectable), fluoxetine (oral), furosemide (oral), haloperidol (oral and injectable), hyoscine butylbromide (oral and injectable), ibuprofen (or alternatives such as naproxen, diclofenac, or meloxicam), lactulose (or alternatives like sorbitol or polyethylene glycol), loperamide (oral), metoclopramide (oral), and metronidazole (oral, which can also be crushed for topical use) are essential medications for palliative care. Morphine, in both oral immediate-release and injectable forms, is critical for managing moderate to severe pain and terminal dyspnea. Naloxone (injectable) is necessary for opioid overdose management. Omeprazole (oral) and ondansetron (oral and injectable) are included for gastrointestinal and antiemetic needs, respectively. Oxygen therapy, paracetamol (oral), and petroleum jelly for wound care are also essential. These items help manage physical symptoms, prevent complications, and reduce caregiver burden. Healthcare providers, including doctors and nurses with basic palliative care training, as well as community health workers (CHWs) when available, are essential for delivering care. Psychological suffering, whether acute or chronic, related to humanitarian emergencies or crises, must be addressed. This includes conditions such as anxiety, depression, confusion, delirium, dementia, and complicated grief. Social workers and psychologists are also critical for providing mental health support. Amitriptyline (oral), dexamethasone (oral and injectable), diazepam (oral and injectable), and diphenhydramine (or alternatives like chlorpheniramine, cyclizine, or dimenhydrinate) are essential medications for managing psychological and neurological symptoms. Haloperidol (oral and injectable) is a first-line treatment for nausea, vomiting, agitation, delirium, and anxiety. Fluoxetine (oral) is the first-line pharmacotherapy for depression and persistent anxiety. Lactulose (or alternatives like sorbitol or polyethylene glycol) is used for constipation management. Doctors, nurses, and CHWs should be trained to provide culturally appropriate psychological support and basic palliative care. Social supports, such as income assistance, food packages, and transportation vouchers, are essential for patients and caregivers living in extreme poverty. Spiritual suffering related to humanitarian emergencies should be addressed by local spiritual counselors when requested by patients or families. This support should align with the patient’s beliefs and cultural needs. Social supports, including funeral cost assistance, are critical for families in low-income settings to alleviate financial and emotional burdens. Morphine, in oral fast-acting and injectable forms, is the most clinically important medication for palliative care. It must be accessible to patients with acute or chronic moderate-to-severe pain, terminal dyspnea, or pain associated with malignancy. Doctors should be trained to prescribe morphine safely and manage its side effects. Opioid storage and record-keeping protocols must be followed to prevent diversion and misuse. Other essential medications include haloperidol (oral and injectable) and fluoxetine (oral), which are safe and effective for managing psychological symptoms in palliative care. Petroleum jelly is crucial for dressing non-healable wounds, and metronidazole powder (made by crushing tablets) is used to reduce odor from infected wounds. In emergencies, adult diapers or alternatives are essential to reduce the risk of skin ulceration and infection. Human resources and training are critical for effective palliative care delivery. Basic palliative care training should be provided to all healthcare workers, including CHWs, to address pain, psychological suffering, and other symptoms. Training should include the diagnosis and treatment of mental, neurological, and substance use disorders, as outlined in WHO guidelines. In humanitarian emergencies, clinicians may encounter complex cases of physical or psychological suffering. When specialist care is unavailable, clinicians with palliative care training should use available resources, including telemedicine, to provide the best possible care. CHWs play a vital role in palliative care by visiting patients at home or in refugee camps, providing emotional support, and reporting uncontrolled symptoms to supervisors. Family caregivers should be trained and equipped to provide basic nursing care, such as wound and mouth care and medication administration. Clinicians should assess and address the social needs of caregivers, who are often women with additional responsibilities and limited resources. Patients with serious or life-limiting conditions should be offered spiritual counseling and the opportunity to prepare legacies for their families, such as letters or memory boxes. Bereavement support, including support groups, should be available for families after a patient’s death. In humanitarian emergencies, patients with advanced chronic illnesses who have lost access to usual healthcare may require palliative care. Efforts should be made to obtain disease-modifying treatments when possible. When such treatments are unavailable or undesired, the focus should shift to comfort and quality of life. Expectant or dying patients should receive comfort-oriented care in a quiet and private location, with family members present. Prognostic understanding should be explored and corrected as needed, with cultural sensitivity. Aggressive efforts must be made to relieve pain and other symptoms, and patients should have access to psychological first aid and focused non-specialized psychological care. In summary, integrating palliative care and symptom relief into humanitarian responses is essential to address the physical, psychological, social, and spiritual suffering of affected individuals.
